patterns.title: External service runtime (a separately deployed backend behind a typed client)
patterns.summary: A separately deployed service — reference: the Rust/Axum runtime lab, an order-rules engine, in its own OCI container — is reached only through one server-only service client: a code-generated OpenAPI contract with generated TS types and drift-checked runtime mirrors, service-enforced bearer auth, request deadlines, one failure kind per cause, request ids and a Server-Timing split. Hardened by measurement: non-blocking stdout logging, SERVICE_TOKEN_PREVIOUS rotation, a 16 KiB head cap, a contract release record with skew diagnosis, cargo-deny, and a 0.1 CPU benchmark profile. Verified locally (container, real client, showcase, controlled lab) and in production on Render Free Frankfurt (end to end, failure paths measured); hosted cold-start and warm percentiles are still unmeasured.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when one responsibility needs its own runtime, release cadence or resource profile — a CPU-heavy engine, a component another product also calls, a language-specific library — and the app must keep working when that process is down.

The motive is the speed of a small computation — the boundary costs ~1 ms on loopback and tens of ms across a network, before any cold start
The browser must call the service directly — that puts the credential or an open endpoint within every visitor's reach

invariants: The browser never calls the service: pages post ids from closed lists (target, preset, drill, patience) and the server owns every URL, credential and request body — no proxy, no CORS

The service's wire types are the contract's only authority: openapi.json is generated from them, tested against the serializer's real behaviour in both directions, and the TS types are generated from it

Runtime validation mirrors are pinned to the generated types at compile time and compared with the spec at test time — every modelled keyword, unknown keywords reported; the client's operation table is pinned to the spec's paths; requests validate closed, responses open

Functional routes require the bearer credential checked by the service itself, in constant time; the service refuses to start without a printable credential of at least 32 characters; liveness is public, gets no credential, and says only 'live'
Every call runs inside the request deadline with a bounded response read and ends in exactly one failure kind; only operations declared idempotent are retried, once, and only when no response arrived

The service bounds what callers can make it hold: request heads must complete in 5 s (idle connections close too) and stay under 16 KiB, connections are capped, and anything it logs from a request is clipped by characters
Logging never holds up the request path: each line is appended to a bounded buffer it never waits on or wakes, a full buffer drops and counts, and shutdown waits for logs at most 1 s
A credential rotates without a refusal window: the service also accepts SERVICE_TOKEN_PREVIOUS, held to the same rules and never equal to the current one, compared on every request

A release names its contract: a contract change without a version bump, or a patch release that changes the contract, is refused by the gate; skew between the running service and the app is reported as a diagnosis only
Credentials and origins appear in no result, log line or error message; the environment is read in one server-only module; plain http carries the credential only to private hosts
The service is optional: one importer, configuration resolved per call, no network work on page load; neither the service nor the client has fault-injection switches
emulation_notes: Give the service its own directory, lockfile, toolchain pin and container definition, and build with that directory as the context — not the repository root.
In a product the service client is a domain named for the service (client, contract, targets, targets.adapter, config); v10r's lab.ts and presets.ts are demo code — do not copy them.

Generate the spec from the service's types and snapshot it; then test the spec against the serializer in both directions — schema generators read attributes, not behaviour (utoipa ignored serde's rename_all_fields and left tagged-enum variants open here).

Prove the drift check by breaking the spec on purpose and asserting where the drift is reported; make it fail on keywords it does not model — a check that silently skips what it cannot read lets the novel break through.
Keep Rust out of the JS gate with a freshness manifest written only when fmt, clippy and tests pass, from hashes taken before they ran, covering the check script itself.
Truncate anything caller-controlled by characters, never bytes, and give the server a header-read timeout — both were real holes in the first version of this service.

Measure the boundary three ways — round trip, the service's own Server-Timing, client overhead — and read the process uptime to recognise a cold start; never claim a language is faster from these numbers.
A breaker fights a free host's cold start (it keeps refusing after the host wakes); add one only for an always-on service.

The log reader is a dependency: println! blocks a worker on a full pipe and panics on a closed one. Write through a bounded buffer one thread drains — and on a fractional CPU do not wake that thread per line: measured at 0.1 CPU, the wake-up cost a fifth of throughput, a 20 ms timed drain beat println! itself.
Measure under the host's envelope (a cgroup CPU quota and memory limit), not only on a workstation: Tokio sized itself to the quota (1 worker) and throttling, not the service, set the tail.

Release-profile tuning (LTO, codegen-units=1, panic=abort) bought 7 µs per call and cost twice the build minutes here; panic=abort would turn a handler panic into a crash. Leave it unless the service is CPU-bound.

Additive is directional: with responses read open, deploy the service before the app that relies on what it adds; expand, migrate, contract for anything that removes. Response enum values are the exception: a reader that validates them strictly turns a new value into a breaking change.
Hash the contract, not the document: drop prose and sort keys before digesting, or every doc-comment edit and generator upgrade reads as a contract change.
Give the costliest public action its own, smaller rate-limit buckets: here a wake check holds a function and the free host for up to 75 s.

~5 ± 2 simultaneous primary choices is a review trigger, never a limit; a flat list stays flat when it is familiar, scannable, repeated, or a comparison.

Gate items by a capability Set on the object and let the builder omit empty groups; the menu never learns node types.
Declare `shortcut` on the menu item and match keyboard events against the same array; never register the same commands in a second global table.
Nest by narrowing intent (Place → When / Where / Map), never because a menu is long; a 'More' bucket of leftovers is the anti-pattern the heuristic exists to catch.
Review with the five-part output (Observation / Reasoning / Opportunity / Possible Direction / Trade-off) and its advisory language; a finding is mandatory only when another requirement makes it so.

invariants: The hard gate is at the tool layer — write/destructive tools return a requiresApproval sentinel; requiresApproval(risk) is the single rule.
Planning is soft guidance, not the gate — shouldRequirePlan only decides whether to instruct the model to plan.

Approval binds execution — the persisted args replay under the scopes frozen at proposal time, against the reviewed baseline, and no model turn follows: the door writes a deterministic execution receipt message.
A run healed to failed('interrupted') is fenced: each step's transaction locks the proposal and refuses unless it is still executing, so a stalled executor cannot commit behind the terminal status.

Undo is compensation, not rollback: one compensating step per receipt, in reverse, each a compare-and-swap against the state the plan left (chained per file) — work the user did since is reported as a conflict, never overwritten.
Undo never widens the model's surface: restores go to the desk domain directly as the asking user, outside executeDeskToolCall and the tool manifest.

The one undo a plan has belongs to the owner of its conversation — checked in the claim itself, so no door can spend it for someone else; a plan whose steps recorded no recovery point is refused rather than 'undone' as a no-op.
emulation_notes: An earlier design (inline ConfirmCard with a model-minted confirmed=false→true handshake) was superseded and never shipped — do not emulate it; the proposal→approve flow is the proven shape.
Record who approved and when at the approve route — the audit trail is the point.
Capture what an undo needs when the step runs (its recovery point, on the receipt, in the same transaction) — reconstructing it later from the current file is guessing.
Key the revert receipt by the forward step it undoes, with a foreign key onto that receipt: a revert of a step that never ran, or a second undo of one step, then cannot be written at all.

invariants: The registry owns the job and its cadence; the platform owns only the clock. A host change moves the clock, never a job.
Registry insertion order IS the sweep's run order — producers before consumers (digest before delivery, rollup before cleanup).
A job rides the shared due-jobs sweep unless it is marked `standalone`, which is reserved for work dominated by external fetches that would blow the sweep's function-duration ceiling.
Every run writes its own `job_execution` row through the one runner, success or failure, so a silent job is visible.
Cron delivery is at-least-once — jobs must be idempotent.
emulation_notes: Jobs are a client of domain modules (multi-client core): a job body should call the same domain functions the UI calls.
Vercel Hobby rejects sub-daily cron schedules at deploy time, so the serverless clock is one daily wake that asks the registry what is due — not one cron entry per job.
Weekly retention sweeps filter on absolute age, so a skipped Sunday is repaired by the next one instead of leaving a gap.

invariants: The core imports no framework, DOM or renderer — only its schema, Valibot and Three.js math — so any caller validates a document exactly as the editor does.
Compatibility comes from PortStandard data the caller supplies; the core names no domain (a gate fails on heating or shelving words in its code).

Operations are pure and deterministic: they return { composition, diagnostics }, never throw, refuse by returning the input unchanged, and the same edits give byte-identical documents (numbers quantised, quaternion sign fixed after quantising).
A coupling says which ports are joined; a conduit says where the pipe or cable runs. Conduit ends always derive from the live port frames.
Mates hold: a mated connect snaps the moving side's whole cluster, a move re-derives the cluster along a spanning tree with no drift, and a ring is accepted only if its mates already hold.
Removing a product removes its couplings and their conduits; no coupling joins one product to itself or the same pair twice; a mate uses its port exclusively.
Findings mean plausibility of declared data only — never certification — and the UI says so on screen.
emulation_notes: Fix the port frame convention first (+Z out, +Y clocking, mate = half turn about +Y) and write the IFC mapping down before any geometry.
Express every compatibility rule as PortStandard data; keep a grep gate for your own domain's words over the core.
Write the scenario test on the pure core before any UI; the browser spec then replays the same steps.
Route conduits by hand with waypoints; add auto-routing (bend-penalised A* on a voxel grid) only for obstacles, many conduits or fitting catalogues.

patterns.title: Optimistic mutation (fold-based rollback, idempotency keys)
patterns.summary: The confirmed value and the pending intents are stored separately and the UI reads the fold of one over the other, so a failed mutation rolls back exactly — even with later mutations applied on top — and a repeated intent executes once.
patterns.when_to_use: Use for reversible, predictable actions where failure is uncommon: rename, toggle, reorder, move, favourite. Never for payments, irreversible deletion, or permission changes.
avoid_when: The action is a payment, an irreversible deletion or a permission change — a rollback cannot restore it
The client cannot predict the server-side outcome, so the optimistic value would be a guess
Failure is common, so the rollback path runs about as often as the confirmed one

alternatives.approach: Pessimistic submit: disable the control and wait for the server's answer
alternatives.prefer_when: the action is irreversible, touches authorization, or has an outcome the client cannot predict

docs.note: The pattern, and what must never go through it

code.note: OptimisticValue: base + pending intents, folded on read

invariants: Optimistic UI never silently diverges permanently from canonical state — the confirmed value is stored separately and is only ever replaced by the server's answer.
Rollback is the removal of one intent from the pending list, never an undo applied in place; later intents stay applied because they are re-folded over the unchanged base.
`apply` is re-run on every read and must be pure.
A retried or double-submitted mutation with the same key executes once — the second caller joins the first.
Security and authorization are never optimistic. The server stays the authority.
emulation_notes: Derive the mutation key from what the intent MEANS (`rename:file-7`), never from when it was issued — a timestamp makes every double-click a distinct intent, which is the thing the key prevents.
Pass the same key as the request's idempotency header and the duplicate protection extends across the network.
`mutate` resolves with an outcome object instead of throwing: a fire-and-forget caller that ignores the promise must not produce an unhandled rejection.
`$effect` never runs under vitest's node environment — unit-test the state machine and prove the reactive wiring in a browser.
patterns.risk: low — client-side state; the server contract is unchanged

avoid_when: The route's data is expensive, highly volatile or unlikely to be used — a preload creates real backend work on a guess
Bandwidth may be constrained, or a speculative load would pollute a cache
No link's cost or follow-through probability differs from the average — the app-wide hover default already covers it

alternatives.approach: SvelteKit's app-wide `data-sveltekit-preload-data="hover"` default alone
alternatives.prefer_when: every link has roughly average cost and probability, so no per-link policy is needed

avoid_when: The collection stays under roughly 200 rows — windowing adds more complexity than it removes

alternatives.prefer_when: the collection is small enough that its DOM, layout and hit-testing cost go unnoticed

invariants: Hidden items create no DOM or layout cost — the saving is layout and hit-testing, not only node count, which is why a long list gets slower to SCROLL and not merely slower to appear.
Keyboard navigation and accessibility stay correct: the list owns focus and moves a roving `aria-activedescendant`, because the rows a user would Tab through mostly do not exist.
Scroll position stays stable — a `scrollTop` past the end clamps instead of stranding the user on a blank screen they cannot scroll out of.
A spacer carries the full data height so the scrollbar describes the list rather than the rendered window.

patterns.title: Hierarchical cache (local → shared → origin, with key scope enforced)
patterns.summary: A read walks outward from process memory to Redis to the origin. The policy declares namespace, TTL, stale window and scope, and `cacheKey` refuses both scope mistakes — a per-user key with no owner, and a shared key handed one.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when reads substantially outnumber writes, the result is expensive and reused, and bounded staleness is acceptable. Not because a cache exists.
avoid_when: The data changes constantly or must be strongly current — the cache becomes a second source of truth
The computation is already cheap, or invalidation would cost more than the work it saves
Reads do not substantially outnumber writes, so entries are invalidated before they are reused

alternatives.approach: Remove or combine the work (drop the fetch, one cheaper query)
alternatives.prefer_when: the cost is avoidable work rather than a reused expensive answer — the decision hierarchy puts removal ahead of caching

alternatives.approach: HTTP / CDN cache headers
alternatives.prefer_when: the response is public and identical for every reader, so the edge can hold it without a key scope

alternatives.approach: A single bounded process-local TTL cache, no shared tier
alternatives.prefer_when: the app runs as one long-lived instance, so there is no second instance for a shared tier to serve

docs.note: The tiers, and key identity as a security boundary

code.note: Policy, key discipline, both tiers, TTL jitter
The nullable Upstash client every consumer must handle
Keeps the style cookie off responses meant for the CDN

invariants: Every cache entry has a declared owner and scope; `cacheKey` throws on a per-user policy with no owner AND on a shared policy handed one — the second is the more dangerous, because it parks a personal value where everyone reads.
A cache key encodes every input that changes the answer. A key that does not is a data leak, not a performance bug.
Freshness lives on the policy (`ttl`, `staleFor`), never argued at the call site; `staleFor` defaults to 0 because serving stale is a decision about correctness.
The local tier is bounded and evicts oldest-used first.
With no Redis configured every shared read is a miss and every write a no-op — a miss is always correct, only slower.
emulation_notes: Store the freshness horizon INSIDE the envelope rather than relying on Redis TTL: Redis expiry is a floor that reclaims memory, and the envelope has to survive a read from the local tier where no Redis TTL exists.
Jitter the per-key TTL. Keys written together otherwise expire together, and synchronised expiry is how a cache becomes a stampede.
Default per-user policies to skipping the local tier: the tier is correct there, but a warm serverless instance accumulates one entry per user it happened to serve.

The CDN is a tier with its own admission rules: Vercel caches a function response only with s-maxage (max-age alone is the browser's) and never one that sets a cookie. v10r's crawler endpoints carried s-maxage and were never cached, because every cookieless crawler was handed a style cookie; the cookie is now kept only on app-shell responses.
patterns.risk: medium — a mis-scoped key is a data leak, which is why the key builder refuses rather than warns

patterns.title: Stale-while-revalidate (and stale-if-error)
patterns.summary: A value past its TTL but inside its stale window is returned immediately and refreshed behind the response; a failing refresh leaves the stale value in place rather than turning a slow dependency into a 500.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when slightly stale is better than waiting: dashboards, feeds, metadata, public content, aggregate counts. Never for authorization, security state or balances requiring strong consistency.
avoid_when: The value is authorization, account security state or a balance needing strong consistency — a stale permission is a wrong permission
The read guards a destructive action, where waiting for a current value beats acting on a slightly stale one
The host freezes instances after the response and offers no after-response hook — a refresh killed halfway leaves the value stale

alternatives.approach: Strict TTL (`staleFor: 0`): recompute on the reader's time once the TTL passes
alternatives.prefer_when: a reader must never see a value past its TTL and paying the recompute latency is acceptable

docs.note: The four outcomes and what must never be stale

code.note: readThrough: fresh / stale / miss / stale-if-error

invariants: The staleness window is explicit per policy — a value with no declared window is never served stale.
Revalidation never blocks the stale response.
A stale value is never mistaken for authoritative security state.
A cold miss with a failing origin throws: there is no stale value to fall back to, so the error is the only honest answer.
emulation_notes: Send the background refresh through the platform's after-response mechanism, not a dangling promise: on a serverless host the instance can be frozen the moment the response returns, and a refresh killed halfway leaves the value stale forever with clean logs.
Only one instance should refresh a shared stale key — combine this with a refresh claim, and note that losing the claim means 'keep serving stale', never 'wait'.
patterns.risk: medium — the staleness window is a correctness decision, not a tuning knob

patterns.title: Singleflight / stampede protection (nobody waits on a lock)
patterns.summary: Concurrent callers for one key share one execution, and across instances a refresh claim stops N instances refreshing the same stale key N times — but a cold caller never blocks on a lock, so a failed leader can never become an outage.
patterns.when_to_use: Use for expensive cache rebuilds, external provider calls, AI calls, aggregate queries and read-model refreshes — anything where a synchronised expiry produces simultaneous identical work.
avoid_when: The work is cheap or never requested concurrently — there is no simultaneous identical work to collapse
Calls that look alike differ in inputs or intent — coalescing would hand a caller someone else's answer
The need is reuse across time — coalescing drops entries on settle; that is a cache's job, not this one's

alternatives.approach: TTL jitter alone
alternatives.prefer_when: the stampede comes from sibling keys expiring together rather than a burst on one key

alternatives.approach: In-process `coalesce` only, without the cross-instance refresh claim
alternatives.prefer_when: the app runs on one instance, or duplicate refreshes across instances are cheap

docs.note: Why a cold caller never waits

code.note: coalesce (in-process) + claimRefresh (cross-instance)

invariants: Only equivalent work is coalesced — same key, same intent — and followers receive the leader's result including its rejection, so nobody silently gets a different answer.
Stampede protection introduces no unbounded waiting: a caller with nothing to serve computes rather than queues.
Every distributed lock carries an expiry, so a leader that dies blocks the next refresh for a bounded time rather than forever.
A Redis failure lets the refresh proceed — the alternative is a value ageing with nobody allowed to renew it.
Coalescing deduplicates, it does not memoize: entries drop on settle.
emulation_notes: The thousand-to-one collapse happens in-process, because a burst lands on an instance rather than on a cluster. The cross-instance claim is the smaller, second-order win.
Reserve the distributed claim for the refresh path. A lock a cold caller waits on turns a slow dependency into a queue.
TTL jitter belongs with this pattern even though it lives in the cache module: desynchronising expiry prevents the stampede that coalescing then has to absorb.
patterns.risk: low — degrades to duplicate work, never to a stall

patterns.title: No-waterfall data loading
patterns.summary: Independent operations execute concurrently; sequential waiting requires a real dependency. The same round trips happen either way — only the waiting is removed, which is why the fix is free.
patterns.when_to_use: Use whenever one request needs several independent resources. Reach for it fourth, after removing the fetch, combining the query, and batching.
avoid_when: The second call needs the first one's result — sequential waiting is correct when the dependency is real
The fetch can be removed, combined into one query or batched — a round trip removed beats a round trip parallelised
The fan-out is an unbounded list — `Promise.all` over it is a load test aimed at your own database

alternatives.approach: Eliminate the fetch
alternatives.prefer_when: the response does not actually need the data

alternatives.approach: Combine into one datastore query
alternatives.prefer_when: the independent reads hit the same store and can be answered by one query

alternatives.approach: Batch equivalent operations (one read by the fetched ids)

invariants: N+1 is defined by SCALING, not by repetition: the same statement twice may be two legitimate lookups, and only a second data size can tell them apart.
A declared budget is the number that was measured on the day it was accepted, never an estimate.
A registered operation costs the same number of round trips at any row count.
Instrumentation is free when nobody is counting — outside a census scope the observer is one context lookup and a return.
The absence of an operation from the registry means nobody measured it, never that it is fine.
A vector query that fell back to a sequential scan is reported as an unused index, ahead of its milliseconds — the two have different fixes.

Count round trips, not milliseconds. A logger that fires before execution has no duration to give, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE answers "why is this slow" far better than a wall clock around a network call.

Keep the per-request ceiling generous. It is a tripwire for the request that suddenly makes ninety queries, not a budget anyone is held to — those are per-operation and asserted where they can be proved.

patterns.summary: Four separate decisions about an unhealthy dependency — should we call it, how much of the pool may it hold, is this work worth doing under pressure, and is this failure worth repeating — kept apart because none of them substitutes for another.

avoid_when: No dependency actually throttles or stalls — breakers, bulkheads and shedding are listed for AI-heavy apps, not CRUD or static sites
You want one resilientCall() wrapper for every call site — its defaults are wrong for most of them
You plan to retry non-idempotent work — a timed-out first attempt may already have succeeded unseen

invariants: Retry storms are impossible: retries draw down the same deadline as the attempt they replace, and every backoff carries full jitter so clients that failed together do not return together.
Failure of one optional capability does not block unrelated capabilities — that is the bulkhead's only job, and it is why one shared pool is not one.
Resilience mechanisms are observable: every refusal names its kind, every shed decision returns its reason, and a breaker logs the count and window that opened it.
Fallback behaviour preserves domain safety. A fallback that widens a permission is not a fallback; degradation may only ever drop privileges.
A refusal is distinct from a failure. `ResilienceError` means the work never ran, so the caller knows a retry is pointless and a fallback is the only useful response.
Only idempotent work is retried. The library cannot check this; the call site can, which is why the judgement lives there.
emulation_notes: Keep the four mechanisms as four modules. Every attempt to merge them produces a 'resilient call' wrapper whose defaults are wrong for most call sites and whose behaviour nobody can predict at the one that matters.

Breaker state belongs in shared storage on serverless — an in-process breaker lets every cold instance independently rediscover the outage, which is the hammering it exists to prevent. Mirror it in memory and write the mirror FIRST, so a failed shared write cannot silently leave the breaker closed.

Skip the half-open state. The first caller after the window is the probe; a true half-open needs a second lock to admit exactly one request, and a handful of duplicate probes is cheaper than that coordination.

A bulkhead bounds one instance and no amount of local bookkeeping changes that. Say so where it is defined — the fleet-wide bound is the platform's concurrency setting and the dependency's connection limit.
Size the queue as a burst absorber, not a backlog. An unbounded queue is latency the caller cannot see and a slower way to exhaust memory.

Shed by priority against pressure that rises BEFORE capacity is reached. Dropping optional work at half load is how the pool avoids being full for the work that is not optional; critical work is never shed for load alone.
Fail-open and fail-closed are both wrong somewhere, so make each call site declare which — `http/rate-limit.ts` splits 'slow' from 'down' for exactly this reason.

invariants: Every timeout value is bounded — there is no operation whose wait is unstated.
A child operation may not exceed its parent's deadline, whatever it asks for. The clamp is in one place so no call site can opt out of it.
A retry consumes the same budget as the attempt it replaces. This is the rule that makes retry-plus-timeout composable instead of multiplicative.
Fallback behaviour is defined per leaf, not inherited. What to return when the budget runs out is domain knowledge.
A deadline bounds the WAIT, not the work: an operation that ignores its AbortSignal still runs to completion, so its promise must carry a catch before anything races it.
emulation_notes: Stamp the deadline at the outermost edge — first or second in the middleware chain. A budget that starts partway through bounds a subset of the request, and every slice taken from it is then wrong in the one direction that matters.
`child(maxMs)` grants the SMALLER of what was asked and what is left. That single clamp, and not the timeouts themselves, is what makes the total bound hold.
`reserveMs` is what stops a leaf from finishing its dependency call with no budget left to use the result. Reserve for the work that happens AFTER the child, not for safety margin.
Every leaf needs a minimum useful budget. Without one, 'the budget ran out' is a boundary condition — the last call starts with a fraction of a millisecond and is abandoned before it can return.
Attach the catch to the abandoned work BEFORE racing it. Once the race rejects nothing is listening, and on Vercel an unhandled rejection can take the process down (SvelteKit #9785).
Adoption is per leaf and incremental. Stamping the budget is cheap; nothing is actually bounded until a leaf takes a child and honours it, so record which leaves have rather than implying coverage.

invariants: Instrumentation does not materially damage performance — a span is one clock pair and one push, and the span list is capped so instrumenting inside a loop degrades to silence rather than to unbounded memory.

`unattributed` is a FLOOR, not a figure: concurrent spans overlap, so their durations can sum past the wall clock and the value clamps at zero. A zero means 'spans covered it', never 'nothing was missed'.
Full span detail is disclosure — it maps internal architecture and hands out a timing oracle — so it goes only to callers who already see internals.
Span names are sanitized to header tokens; a raw name would inject a delimiter and corrupt every field after it.
Coverage is stated, not implied: prerendered routes never reach the handler on a CDN-served deployment.

patterns.title: Untrusted-content boundary (the lethal trifecta, one rule per leg)
patterns.summary: Every AI tool declares where its result comes from and whether it can send data out; user-origin results reach the model as one escaped <untrusted-content> element (this turn via toModelOutput, replayed turns via the history), external-reach tools must be approval-gated, and model output renders no image or unlisted link — a gate test holds all three legs.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when an assistant reads content a user or third party wrote — files, retrieved documents, web pages, tool output — and can also act or answer with links.
avoid_when: The assistant only ever reads a corpus you own and has no tools that act or send — there is no untrusted leg to bound
You need to detect injection attempts for moderation; this bounds and removes legs, it does not classify

alternatives.approach: Dual-LLM or CaMeL-style quarantine (a privileged planner never sees untrusted text)
alternatives.prefer_when: the assistant must act on untrusted content and also hold external tools

alternatives.approach: Injection classifiers (Prompt Guard, Lakera)
alternatives.prefer_when: you want telemetry on attempts on top of the structural rule, never instead of it

patterns.title: AI eval regression suite (golden set, deterministic graders over the turn trace, floor ratchet)
patterns.summary: A committed golden set of questions, each with the facts its recorded turn must show — citations surfaced not recalled, the right tool called, no forbidden tool, an approval stop, no invented command — graded by pure functions over the turn trace, with a pass-rate floor that only rises; live runs go through the app's own routes against a local dev server.
patterns.when_to_use: Use when prompts, retrieval, tools or models change often and unit tests mock the model, so quality regressions would ship unnoticed.
avoid_when: Turns are not recorded — without a trace of tools and citations the graders have nothing deterministic to read
The quality question is open-ended style or tone that no fact in the trace can decide

alternatives.approach: LLM-as-judge suites (promptfoo, Braintrust, LangSmith)
alternatives.prefer_when: the facts to check are judgments no trace field records, and the judge is calibrated against human labels

alternatives.approach: Offline retrieval benchmarks (Acc@1, Recall@k)
alternatives.prefer_when: only the retrieval layer changes and no model call is needed to score it

patterns.title: PIM Excel workflow with AI agents (profile, proposed recipe, deterministic run, target check)
patterns.summary: Supplier Excel/CSV product exports become a target's import sheet without the model touching a row: the agent reads a bounded column profile and proposes a typed transform recipe, a column walk refuses imagined columns, code runs the recipe over every row (unreadable values left unchanged and listed by source line), and a target-schema check over the full output is the definition of done — in a bounded propose → run → check → revise loop, in-app, or from a terminal agent with the `pim` program over plain job folders (no git, no repo; one dated output folder per run).
patterns.when_to_use: Use when product data (supplier exports, ERP dumps, marketplace templates) arrives as spreadsheets that must be analysed and transformed into a fixed import format, the same kind of file recurs, or the sheet is too large to check by eye.
avoid_when: A one-off cleanup of a few hundred rows nobody will send again — editing it in Excel is faster than writing a target schema
The transformation needs judgement per row (rewriting marketing copy, translating descriptions) — a recipe of typed ops cannot express it; that is a per-row generation job with its own review
The data already lives in a PIM with its own import mapping and validation — configure that instead of running a second engine beside it

alternatives.approach: Ask the model to rewrite the sheet (code interpreter, spreadsheet copilots)
alternatives.prefer_when: the sheet is small, the result is looked at once, and nobody needs to reproduce or audit it

alternatives.approach: A PIM's or ETL tool's import mapping (Akeneo, Pimcore, Talend, Power Query)
alternatives.prefer_when: the organisation already runs one and the mapping is maintained by people who own it

alternatives.approach: Hand-written transformation script per supplier
alternatives.prefer_when: the logic needs real code (lookups against an ERP, conditional derivations) beyond the op vocabulary

invariants: The model never writes a cell; its only output is a recipe, and a recipe only does what its typed ops do.
A recipe that reads a column which does not exist when its op runs is refused whole, before any row is touched.
An op never guesses: a value it cannot read is left unchanged and reported with its source line.
Done means the target-schema check over every row passes, not that the model says so.
Every value stays text from file to file; nothing becomes a number unless an op says so.
A run never overwrites an earlier one; each output folder carries the recipe and target that produced it.
emulation_notes: Write the target schema first, from the destination's import documentation — it is the grader, so it must not come from the supplier file or the model.
Give the agent a profile bounded by columns (counts, top values, shape, a few clipped rows), never the rows; the prompt then costs the same for 40 rows and 40,000.
Keep the op vocabulary small and typed, and walk the column set through it before running; that one check catches the plan built on an imagined column.
Read .xlsx numbers as their stored digits and write every cell as text, or GTINs and article numbers are corrupted on the next save.
Hand over a workbook with the issues and the change log beside the output, and keep the recipe per supplier — next month's export is a re-run, not a new conversation.
Assume office users have folders and Excel, not git: one job folder per supplier found by file name, a dated output folder per run as the history, and the tool shipped as a single compiled file.
patterns.risk: low — the engine is pure and every run is reproducible from input + recipe; the residual risk is a recipe that runs cleanly but maps a value wrongly (e.g. a colour), which the change log and a person's review are there to catch
